task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent H2-H1 change
measurement reliability of half-based difference metrics
methodological_questions: Is a team's effect on opponents' second-half minus first-half scoring change stable across seasons (year-over-year ICC) and across random game halves (split-half reliability)?
How many team-seasons are needed to detect a persistent defensive trait in a half-difference metric at a useful power?
Do selection on extreme prior-season values (regression to the mean) or half-difference construction artifacts produce an apparent persistent effect?
Does the estimate survive controls for opponent quality, pace, and free-throw or garbage-time composition?

historical_evidence.finding: Split-half reliability of connector teammate-path quality Q_p (player-season, n=102): Pearson r=+0.215, Spearman-Brown about 0.355, ICC 0.216 with 78.4% of variance within-player. [prior work] concludes Q_p is too unstable to treat as a scoutable trait; most variance is half-to-half. This concerns a player-level metric, not team defense.

Ranked playsheet counter validation over 10 series (n=665): Spearman rho=-0.0639, p=0.0997 (no full-rank signal). Kruskal-Wallis H=32.97, p=2.7e-05. BEST (mean 1.257, n=56) vs AVOID (mean 1.092, n=160), Mann-Whitney p=0.004. Trigger accuracy rho=0.4525 (n=121). Concerns counter-strategy ranking after a defense drops a play type, not a team's trait.

Foul-trouble sequencing test: including free throws gave lag-1 ATT=+0.204 (CI +0.163 to +0.245), but free-throw share was 41.8% treated vs 9.9% control. Excluding free throws, lag-1 was +0.0486 [-0.0060, +0.0991], permutation p=0.0655; lags 2 and 3 were negative. No lag cleared CI, permutation and placebo together.

Possession Control Index incremental R2 over ORtg (n=120 team-seasons, OOS 2025-26 with 30 teams): headline gain dR2=+0.139 was attributed to leakage tracking DRtg (corr(leakage, DRtg)=+0.894). Offensive-control components added only +0.005 R2 beyond ORtg. The baseline omitted defense by construction (Net=ORtg-DRtg).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating a half-split difference-type metric as a stable player trait
failed_approaches.why: Recorded reliability was low (r=0.215, Spearman-Brown about 0.355; ICC 0.216), so most variance was within-player half-to-half noise; [prior work] classifies the question as unanswerable with the data and design.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Ranking playsheet counters by predicted second-half advantage after a defensive drop
failed_approaches.why: Full-rank Spearman was null (rho=-0.064, p=0.10). Only a pairwise BEST>AVOID contrast was significant, [prior work] cites small sample, low measurement reliability and leakage, and the outcome is inconclusive.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Foul-trouble lag effect on opponent PPP including free-throw possessions
failed_approaches.why: The apparent effect was a mechanical artifact of free-throw share imbalance (41.8% vs 9.9%); the apples-to-apples estimate was not significant.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Team-level efficiency model claiming incremental R2 for control metrics over ORtg
failed_approaches.why: The headline gain was leakage tracking DRtg (corr +0.894); the true offensive-control increment was +0.005 R2.

evidence_establishes: Half-based and difference-based player or team metrics in this project have shown low split-half reliability ([prior work][prior work]), so a persistent-trait claim needs explicit reliability estimation before any inference.
Apparent effects built on half-split or free-throw-laden possession counts have been artifacts (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]), so construction checks are required.
Counter-strategy rankings from this project have not produced a clean full-rank signal ([prior work][prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: No returned record estimates the reliability of a team defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change. The question is not answered by any retrieved study.
No returned record gives a team-level ICC, year-over-year correlation or power calculation for this metric with 120 team-seasons.
The retrieved results were truncated at '[cut; read_family for the full text]' and I did not call read_family, so details beyond the summaries shown are unverified.
own_inferences: The 120 team-seasons are plausibly 4 seasons x 30 teams (2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons). Playoff data would add correlated and small-sample noise, so the primary test should use regular seasons only.

An H2-H1 difference per team-season is a noisy difference of two half-game means. Its between-team signal is likely small relative to within-team game noise, so a reliability ICC near or below the 0.3-0.5 range is plausible.
Team defense effects on H2-H1 are confounded with opponent quality, pace, and late-game fouling and garbage-time patterns, which the retrieved records do not address.
uncertainties: Actual between-team variance of the H2-H1 defensive effect is unknown and could be near zero.
Whether 2025-26 regular-season data (complete from 2026-04-13) is usable as a holdout with the same pipeline is not verified.
Multiple defensive metrics and play-type cuts would inflate false positives; the number of candidate metrics is not stated.
Historical records are project-internal and some use different metrics, so transfer to this question is indirect.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records show low reliability of a half-split metric ([prior work][prior work]) and artifacts from construction flaws (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]). These push the decision from an unconditional proceed to proceed_with_changes: reliability must be estimated first, with a pre-specified gate, and free-throw and leakage checks built in. No record tests the question directly, so the evidence does not support a positive claim.

blocking_constraints.text: H2-H1 difference per team-season is a noisy statistic; prior half-split reliability in this project was low ([prior work][prior work]), so a stable trait may not be detectable.
120 team-seasons (about 30 teams over 4 seasons) gives limited power to detect a modest between-team variance component, and the year-over-year ICC will have wide intervals.
Opponent quality, pace, free-throw share and garbage-time effects can mimic a defensive effect on H2-H1 change; the retrieved records show free-throw artifacts (FAM:[prior work]).

prior_work.summary: No retrieved study estimates the reliability of team defense on opponents' H2-H1 change. Related records give a reliability warning for half-split player metrics ([prior work][prior work]), counter-ranking nulls ([prior work][prior work]), and artifact patterns from free-throw and leakage construction (FAM:[prior work], [prior work][prior work]).

risks.text: Half-to-half noise likely dominates the H2-H1 difference; the trait claim requires a reliability estimate, not just a mean effect.
About 120 team-seasons may be too few to detect a modest persistent variance component after shrinkage.
Opponent strength, pace, free-throw share and garbage time may produce spurious defense effects on H2-H1.
Selecting teams with extreme prior-season H2-H1 suppression and testing persistence will bias the estimated persistence upward through regression to the mean.
Rule and pace changes across 2022-23 to 2025-26 can shift the H2-H1 distribution by season, so year-over-year correlation may reflect league-wide drift.
Using full-season or playoff data to define a team's defensive effect and then testing it on the same games would leak the outcome; the PCI record shows this risk ([prior work][prior work]).
Testing several H2-H1 definitions, splits and defensive metrics raises the false-positive rate.
Without a placebo-half or shuffled-game control, a positive persistence result cannot be distinguished from construction artifacts.

design.estimand: Between-team variance share (ICC) and year-over-year correlation of each team's defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 scoring change, after opponent-quality, pace and free-throw adjustment.
design.unit: Team-season (defense), with opponent-game possessions as the within-unit data.
design.sample: Regular seasons 2022-23 to 2024-25 (90 team-seasons) for estimation, with 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13) as a holdout (30 team-seasons). Playoffs excluded from the primary test.
design.power: Pre-run simulation using the observed within-team game variance to find the minimum detectable ICC at 80% power over 120 team-seasons. Proceed to the substantive test only if simulated power is adequate; otherwise report the question as underpowered.
design.controls: Adjust for opponent offensive and defensive strength, pace, free-throw attempts per possession, garbage-time indicator (margin over 20 late), and home/away. Use mixed-effects shrinkage. Define H1/H2 identically across seasons; exclude overtime.
design.falsification: (a) Shuffle game order within team-season and recompute ICC, which should fall to zero; (b) use a placebo half split (e.g., odd/even minutes); (c) show the effect vanishes when free throws are excluded, as in FAM:[prior work]. Reject if placebo ICC is not near zero.
design.multiplicity: One primary test (year-over-year ICC of the pre-specified defensive metric). Secondary metrics and splits are reported as exploratory with Holm correction.
design.decision_rule: Call the defensive effect a reliable team trait only if the 2025-26 holdout year-over-year correlation has a bootstrap 95% lower bound above 0.2, split-half Spearman-Brown reliability is above 0.5, and the placebo ICC CI includes 0. Otherwise report as not reliable or inconclusive, not as an artifact.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game files as pulled on 2026-10-06; 2025-26 regular season complete from 2026-04-13; playoff rows excluded; code and feature definitions frozen before analysis.
